questions.q: What does a clustered index determine?
options: The actual physical order the table's rows are stored in on disk
The number of nonclustered indexes allowed
Which columns can be used in a WHERE clause
Only the order results are displayed in, with no effect on storage
questions.explain: Because it defines physical storage order, a table can have only one clustered index.

questions.q: How many clustered indexes can a single table have?
options: Exactly two
Unlimited
At most one
Zero — clustered indexes are deprecated
questions.explain: The data can only be physically sorted one way, so only one clustered index is possible per table.

questions.q: What extra step does looking up a row via a nonclustered index require, compared to the clustered index?
options: Find the entry in the index, then follow a pointer back to the actual row
A full table scan is always required afterward
No extra step — they work identically
The row must be manually re-sorted first
questions.explain: A nonclustered index is a separate structure holding a pointer, not the actual row data itself.

questions.q: What are the three characteristics of a good clustering key?
options: Narrow, unique, and ever-increasing
Wide, duplicated, and randomly ordered
Text-based, nullable, and variable-length
Large, composite, and frequently updated
questions.explain: This is exactly why an auto-incrementing integer primary key is such a common, effective clustering key choice.

questions.q: Why do SARGable predicates (Lesson 87) matter for indexes specifically?
options: Non-SARGable predicates delete existing indexes
They let SQL Server actually use clustered/nonclustered index structures; a non-SARGable predicate forces a scan regardless of how well-designed the indexes are
SARGable predicates automatically create new indexes
Indexes only matter for nonclustered indexes, not clustered ones
questions.explain: This ties Lesson 87 directly to this lesson — good indexes are wasted without SARGable predicates to actually use them.
